title: IP vs BP vs USP vs EP Grade: What's the Difference and Which Should You Use?
metaTitle: IP vs BP vs USP vs EP Grade Explained | Surravi Phharma
metaDescription: What is the difference between IP, BP, USP, and EP grades in pharmaceuticals? Learn which grade your formulation needs and why it matters for...
excerpt: One of the most common questions from pharmaceutical formulators in India is: which pharmacopoeial grade should I specify — IP, BP, USP, or EP? The answer depends on where your product is registered, who your end customer is, and what your formulation requires.

content.text: One of the most common questions we receive from pharmaceutical formulators, procurement managers, and nutraceutical brands is: which grade should I order — IP, BP, USP, or EP? The short answer is that all four are equivalent in terms of purity and quality, but each is published by a different national or regional pharmacopoeia. The right choice depends on where your product will be registered and sold..
What is a Pharmacopoeia?

A pharmacopoeia is an official compendium of standards for medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients, published by a government or regulatory authority. It defines the tests, procedures, and acceptance criteria that a pharmaceutical ingredient must meet to be considered of acceptable quality. Using pharmacopoeial-grade materials is a core requirement of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) worldwide.
IP — Indian Pharmacopoeia

The Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) is published by the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare. For any pharmaceutical product registered and sold in India under Schedule M of the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, excipients and APIs listed in the IP must comply with IP standards. IP is the default required grade for domestic Indian pharmaceutical formulations. If your product is only for the Indian market, IP grade is sufficient and is usually the most economical option.
BP — British Pharmacopoeia

The British Pharmacopoeia (BP) is published by the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). BP grade is required for pharmaceutical products registered in the UK, Commonwealth countries, and many African and Middle Eastern markets that follow British pharmaceutical standards. BP grade materials are also widely accepted in India for export formulations and by multinational pharmaceutical companies operating manufacturing facilities in India.
EP — European Pharmacopoeia

The European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur. or EP) is published by the European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines (EDQM) and is the mandatory standard for pharmaceutical products registered in all 37 European Pharmacopoeia member states. EP grade is required for products exported to the European Union. Importantly, the BP monographs for most excipients are aligned with EP monographs — so a material meeting BP generally meets EP as well.
USP — United States Pharmacopeia

The USP-NF (United States Pharmacopeia – National Formulary) is published by the United States Pharmacopoeial Convention and is required for pharmaceutical products registered with the US FDA. USP grade is mandatory for any product exported to the United States or manufactured to FDA-approved specifications. USP is also widely adopted globally by innovator pharmaceutical companies as their voluntary internal quality standard. For parenteral (injectable) formulations and high-purity applications, USP grade often has the most stringent endotoxin and particulate matter requirements.
Are IP, BP, EP, and USP grades chemically the same?

For most common pharmaceutical excipients and active ingredients, the quality of the material meeting any of these standards is functionally equivalent — all specify high purity, defined assay ranges, and strict limits on impurities, heavy metals, and microbiological contamination. The differences between pharmacopoeias are primarily in the specific test methods and acceptance criteria used to verify quality, not in the actual purity of the material itself.

However, there are cases where specifications differ meaningfully. Mannitol IP and USP both require 98.0–102.0% assay, but differ in specific test methodologies. Some newer EP monographs have stricter elemental impurity limits following ICH Q3D guidelines. Always review the specific monograph for your ingredient if regulatory precision matters.
Which grade should you specify for Indian pharmaceutical manufacturing?

For domestic Indian formulations — IP grade is sufficient and is the most cost-effective choice. For export to UK and Commonwealth markets — specify BP. For export to Europe — specify EP (or BP, which is harmonised with EP for most monographs). For export to the USA or FDA-regulated formulations — specify USP. For multi-market products — specify USP/BP/EP, as these are the most globally accepted standards. Many manufacturers in India specify multi-pharmacopoeial compliance (e.g., IP/BP/USP compliant) to maintain flexibility.

title: How to Read a Certificate of Analysis (COA): Step-by-Step Guide for Pharma Buyers
metaTitle: How to Read a COA: Pharma Step-by-Step Guide | Surravi
metaDescription: Learn how to read a Certificate of Analysis (COA) for pharma excipients and APIs: key sections, a checklist and red flags. Guide from a Hyderabad supplier.
excerpt: A Certificate of Analysis (COA) is the proof that a batch of pharmaceutical ingredient meets its specification. This step-by-step guide shows Indian formulators and procurement teams how to read a COA, verify it, and spot red flags before accepting a batch.

content.text: A Certificate of Analysis (COA) is a batch-specific quality document that shows a pharmaceutical ingredient was tested and met its stated specification. If you buy excipients, APIs, vitamins or food-grade ingredients, reading the COA correctly is one of the simplest ways to protect your product quality and pass audits. Many buyers only check that a COA is attached. This guide explains how to actually read one, step by step.
What is a Certificate of Analysis (COA) in pharmaceuticals?

A COA is issued by the manufacturer's quality control laboratory for one specific batch or lot. It lists every test performed, the acceptance limit for each test, and the actual result obtained. It is not a general product brochure. A valid COA must be traceable to the material you received through the batch number printed on the drum, bag or carton label.
Why is a COA important for pharmaceutical manufacturers?

Pharmaceutical and nutraceutical manufacturers work under GMP, where every raw material must be shown to meet its specification before use. The COA is the first piece of evidence in that chain. It supports your incoming material release, your batch manufacturing records, and your customer and regulatory audits. Without a proper COA, a material generally cannot be approved for production.
What information should a COA contain?
Header details: product name, grade or pharmacopoeia (IP, BP, EP or USP), batch or lot number, manufacturing date, expiry or retest date, and the manufacturer's name and address.

Tests and specifications: a table of tests such as description, identification, assay, loss on drying, pH, heavy metals, residue on ignition and microbial limits. The specification column shows the acceptable range, and the result column shows the value measured for this batch.
Test method reference: the method used for each test, usually a reference to the relevant pharmacopoeial monograph or a validated in-house method.
Approval: a signature or authorisation from a quality control or quality assurance representative, with a date. An unsigned or undated COA carries little weight in an audit.
How to read a COA step by step
Step 1 - Match the batch number. Compare the batch number on the COA with the batch number on the containers you received. If they do not match, the COA does not belong to your material.

Step 2 - Confirm the grade. Check that the pharmacopoeia named on the COA is the one you ordered. If you ordered USP grade, a COA that only refers to an in-house specification is not enough. Our guide on IP, BP, USP and EP grades explains how these standards differ.

Step 3 - Compare every result with its limit. Each result must fall inside the stated specification. Pay closest attention to assay, related substances or impurities, heavy metals and microbial limits.
Step 4 - Check the dates. Make sure the manufacturing date and expiry or retest date are realistic and leave enough shelf life for your production schedule.
Step 5 - Look for numerical values. Good COAs report actual figures, for example an assay of 99.6%, not just the word Complies. Numbers let your team track batch-to-batch consistency.
Step 6 - Verify the authorisation. Confirm the COA is signed and dated by the manufacturer's QC or QA department, and that the manufacturer details are present.
COA red flags every buyer should watch for

Pause and ask your supplier for clarification if you see any of the following: no batch number or a mismatched batch number; no manufacturer name or address; no test methods listed; results that sit exactly on the specification limit for every test; a pharmacopoeia edition different from what you specified; a blurry, edited or heavily copied document; or missing signature and date.
Manufacturer COA vs supplier COA: which one should you ask for?

Importers and distributors normally pass on the original manufacturer's COA, and this is what most regulated buyers expect because it traces the batch back to the site that made and tested it. Many quality teams also run their own incoming quality control tests on top of the COA, particularly for critical materials. A COA lowers risk but does not replace your own sampling and verification procedures.
COA vs MSDS vs TDS: what is the difference?

A COA reports the test results of one specific batch. A Technical Data Sheet (TDS) describes the general properties, specifications and typical uses of a product. A Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS or SDS) covers hazards, safe handling, storage and emergency measures. Most supplier qualification files include all three.
Which documents should you request along with the COA?

Depending on your product and regulatory needs, ask for the MSDS, the TDS, a copy of the manufacturer's GMP or manufacturing licence, and a declaration of origin. Requesting these during supplier qualification saves time later, especially during customer or regulatory audits.
Frequently asked questions about COA
Is a COA mandatory for pharmaceutical raw materials? For GMP-regulated manufacturing, a COA for each batch is a standard requirement for accepting and releasing raw materials.
Can one COA be used for multiple batches? No. A COA is specific to one batch or lot. Each new batch needs its own COA.
What does retest date mean on a COA? The retest date is the date after which the material should be re-tested to confirm it still meets its specification before use.
What if the COA result is outside the specification? Do not use the material. Contact the supplier, quarantine the batch and follow your deviation or out-of-specification procedure.
Can I get a COA before placing an order? Yes. Reputable suppliers can share a sample COA or the current batch COA so you can review it before you buy.
